Tailoring defect chemistry of 2D transition metal dichalcogenides towards high-performance zinc-based batteries
abstract: Zinc–based batteries (ZBBs) have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation energy storage. However, their practical implementation remains hindered by the inherently sluggish electrochemical kinetics and the inferior cycling durability of cathode materials. Layered transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have garnered extensive attention as cathodes for ZBBs, owing to their layered frameworks that facilitate Zn 2+ intercalation/de-intercalation. Nevertheless, pristine TMDs inherently suffer from electrochemically inert basal planes and low electronic conductivity, thus compromising their electrochemical performance. Defect engineering has emerged as an effective strategy to fundamentally enhance the electrochemical activity of TMDs. This review comprehensively outlines the recent advances of defect-engineered TMDs for ZBBs, beginning with an overview of classifications, charge storage mechanisms, and key issues associated with reaction kinetics and interfacial stability of ZBBs. Subsequently, the structural features, synthesis methods, and application potential of TMDs as cathodes across diverse ZBBs are summarized. Particular emphasis is placed on the “defect chemistry–electronic structure–electrochemical performance” paradigm to elucidate structure–property relationships of TMDs. We critically analyze the evolution from single to coupled defects and correlate defect configurations with electrochemical activity and stability. Finally, the remaining challenges and future prospects for the rational design of defect-engineered TMDs for ZBBs toward large-scale applications are discussed.

Advances in biomass-derived shape-stabilized bio-phase change materials for building thermal management and emerging machine learning approaches
abstract: Phase change materials (PCMs) are becoming popular material for thermal energy storage in many applications especially in buildings. PCM integrated into buildings can regulate indoor temperatures and reduce energy consumption. However, most conventional PCMs are nonrenewable petroleum-based materials which are also associated to high CO2 emissions during production. Bio-based PCMs (Bio-PCMs) and agricultural biomass derived shape stabilized bio PCMs (Bio-SSPCMs) are considered sustainable promising alternatives as they are considered biodegradable, low cost, environmentally friendly, and can offer diverse melting points and latent heat capacities. This review provides a comprehensive assessment of Bio-PCMs and Bio-SSPCMs, covering their classifications, thermophysical and chemical properties, preparation and activation methods, agricultural biomass carriers, building integration, cost analysis, and the role of machine learning in their optimization. Results showed that Bio-SSPCM using agricultural biochar can effectively prevent leakage, enhance thermal conductivity up to 184%, and improve thermal energy storage performance. Moreover, Bio-SSPCMs have the potential to reduce building indoor temperature by up to 6.5 °C. Further results showed that machine learning (ML) has an effective role in predicting thermal performance, thermophysical properties, phase change kinetics, and degradation behavior. Although there is no single optimal ML model that can be used, based on the literature artificial neural networks and random forest models demonstrate superior performance compared to other ML models.

Degradation of metallic interconnects in solid oxide electrolysis cells: mechanisms, materials challenges, and design strategies
abstract: With their unmatched electrical-to-chemical conversion efficiency, solid oxide electrolysis cells (SOECs) are increasingly recognized as a cornerstone technology for the green energy transition. Realizing this potential, however, critically depends on the durability of key stack components, most notably the metallic interconnects. Metallic interconnects in solid oxide electrolysis cells must withstand aggressive high-temperature, dual-atmosphere conditions. This review evaluates the current state of metallic interconnect materials for SOEC stacks, drawing on the more extensive Solid Oxide Fuel Cell (SOFC) literature while highlighting key differences. The analysis is structured around oxidation behavior on the oxygen and hydrogen/steam sides and dual-atmosphere effects, with emphasis on the interplay between chromia scale growth, chromium volatilization, and breakaway oxidation and their impact on interconnect lifetime and electrical performance. Key distinctions in SOEC operation including high steam content, reversed current polarity, and dual-atmosphere exposure are highlighted, revealing conditions where SOFC-based insights fail or require modification. The review evaluates alloy design and coating strategies and identifies critical knowledge gaps, particularly in low-temperature steam-side corrosion and dual-atmosphere degradation, outlining priorities for SOEC-specific material development
